root.title: With a Little Help
root.gist: Cory Doctorow's story collection argues that pervasive data-surveillance corrupts institutions and people even when they begin with good intentions.
root.question: With a Little Help — how does constant surveillance change the people and systems that build it? (several linked stories)

children.title: Front matter and contents
children.gist: Title page, table of contents, dedication, publication history, and a note on typos introduce the collection before the stories begin.

children.title: Title and contents
children.gist: The book's title page and table of contents list.

children.title: Dedication
children.gist: A short dedication to friends.

children.title: Publication history
children.gist: A list of where each story originally appeared.

children.title: Note about typos
children.gist: The author invites readers to report typos for correction and credit.

children.title: Introduction by Jonathan Coulton
children.gist: Coulton argues that the internet, not space travel, is the disruptive force shaping the future, and that Doctorow's fiction confronts its messy consequences while testing new publishing models himself.
children.question: Introduction — why does Coulton think the internet, not space travel, defines the future this book addresses? (an introduction)

children.title: Science fiction's missed future
children.gist: Coulton recalls expecting space travel to define the future but argues the internet turned out to be the real unanticipated, transformative force.

children.title: Doctorow's relevant fiction
children.gist: He says Doctorow's stories matter because they grapple directly with surveillance, corporate power, and the uncertain economics of being a creator online.

children.title: An experiment in publishing
children.gist: The book itself tests new models of selling and sharing creative work, using Creative Commons licensing, multiple price points, and public transparency.

children.title: Coulton's own Creative Commons story
children.gist: Coulton explains how discovering Creative Commons let him release his music freely and build a career, convincing him that sharing and borrowing are how creation actually works.

children.title: What Doctorow might be missing
children.gist: Coulton closes by wondering what blind spot Doctorow himself has about the future, suggesting the real corner ahead is still unknown.

children.title: The Things That Make Me Weak and Strange Get Engineered Away
children.gist: A monk in a data-surveillance order leaves his cloistered campus to chase a data anomaly, and in confronting the outside world's compromises he chooses to return and extend the same watched, instrumented life.
children.question: The Things That Make Me Weak and Strange Get Engineered Away — why does Lawrence choose to go back inside after seeing the outside world? (a short story)

children.title: An anomaly inside the Order
children.gist: Monk Lawrence and his colleague Gerta trace a tampered data-stream to a vanished brother, Zbigniew Krotoski, whose empty room has been scrubbed of all trace.

children.title: Leaving the campus
children.gist: An old gatekeeper warns Lawrence, stepping outside for the first time in sixteen years, that the real world is dangerous and that he should listen before acting.

children.title: Remembering why he joined
children.gist: Lawrence recalls his unraveling life in New York before the Order, when his intelligence made him unemployable and miserable until he found relief in constant self-monitoring.

children.title: First contact with the Securitat
children.gist: Armed Securitat officers violently search Lawrence on the street, teaching him that any unexplained gesture outside can be read as a threat in this policed world.

children.title: Posy and the logic of universal guilt
children.gist: A stranger named Posy shelters Lawrence and argues that everyone is guilty of something and that surveillance culture, including the Order's own work for the Securitat, enables arbitrary disappearances like that of her neighbor.

children.title: Tracking Zbigkrot's trail
children.gist: Lawrence pieces together Zbigkrot's history and searches for his vanished sister Anja, learning from neighbors and a phone call with Gerta that honesty, not stealth, is the better approach outside.

children.title: Recruited by Randy
children.gist: A charming stranger named Randy leads Lawrence to an underground dinner, reveals himself as Securitat, and explains that the organization recruits through everyone's inevitable guilt rather than pure coercion.

children.title: Interrogation and acceptance
children.gist: After trying to flee and being tasered, Lawrence is interrogated by Randy, who argues the surveillance system is permanent and persuades him that joining its workforce is the only realistic choice.

children.title: Choosing to stay watched
children.gist: Returning to a campus now fitted with a Securitat-monitored pan, Lawrence says goodbye to Gerta and accepts that he, like Zbigkrot before him, will live and work inside the same surveilled system forever.

children.title: Afterword to the story
children.gist: Doctorow explains the story grew from a conversation about where disaffected, brilliant misfits would have gone in earlier eras: a monastery.

children.title: The Right Book
children.gist: Across three future eras, a bookseller and the young writer he champions show that getting people to love reading requires putting books where new readers already are, not just in bookshops.
children.question: The Right Book — how does the right book reach a reader who doesn't already love reading? (a three-part future history)

children.title: Arthur's shop and the hand-made books
children.gist: Shopkeeper Arthur sells expensive crowd-sourced story anthologies called The Story So Far, and a teenage writer named Chloe Autumn convinces him to stock her own cheaper, self-bound editions.

children.title: Chloe decades later
children.gist: Seventy-five years on, an aged Chloe Autumn now runs the bookshop empire Arthur built, which succeeded by putting curated, locally relevant books into everyday shops where young non-readers already went.

children.title: A character wakes to sell books
children.gist: Far in the future, a character generated from The Story So Far is instantiated to meet a specific young reader, showing storytelling itself has become fully personalized and automated.

children.title: Afterword to the story
children.gist: Doctorow explains the story was commissioned around an editor's argument that losing small book distributors to grocers and pharmacies has cut off how new readers discover their first beloved book.

children.title: Other People's Money
children.gist: A sculptor who makes art from discarded electronics explains to a venture capitalist why her small-scale, capital-free business model beats the boom-bust VC world that once rejected her.
children.question: Other People's Money — why does Gretl refuse to scale her business with venture capital? (a dialogue)

children.title: A VC seeks out Gretl
children.gist: A young venture capitalist tries to court sculptor Gretl at her market stall, unaware she was burned by VCs decades earlier.

children.title: Gretl's history of failed startups
children.gist: Gretl recounts two previous ventures that failed to attract capital despite real traction, due to bad timing, bad luck, and ageism rather than bad ideas.

children.title: Art from salvaged electronics
children.gist: Gretl shows the VC her sculptures made from discarded phones and gadgets, explaining that reclaiming obsolete tech objects restores an emotional value mass production destroyed.

children.title: Why scale doesn't help
children.gist: Gretl argues that materials, design, fabrication and retail all already scale cheaply through salvage and automation, so outside capital would add nothing she actually needs.

children.title: Afterword to the story
children.gist: Doctorow says Forbes commissioned a piece on the future of entrepreneurship, prompting this dialogue about how little capital a modern creator-business really needs.

children.title: Scroogled
children.gist: An ex-Googler discovers that Google's search and email data have been quietly weaponized by government and corporate interests, trapping him into joining the very surveillance machine that destroyed his friend.
children.question: Scroogled — how does a well-meaning tech company become an instrument of state surveillance? (a short story)

children.title: Interrogated at the border
children.gist: Returning from Mexico, Greg is detained for hours as a Customs officer interrogates him using years of his old Google search and email history.

children.title: Maya explains the googlecleaner
children.gist: His friend Maya, still at Google, reveals that search results are secretly personalized to flag people as suspects and that she built a secret tool to scrub profiles of flagged colleagues.

children.title: The tool is weaponized
children.gist: Maya discovers her googlecleaner is now being used by a political lobbying firm to smear and launder candidates' reputations, and realizes she and Greg are being watched for it.

children.title: Maya flees, Greg is co-opted
children.gist: Maya and her girlfriend flee the country while Greg is blackmailed by a Google-linked operative into joining a secret unit that formalizes profile manipulation for political and state clients.

children.title: Deputized into the surveillance state
children.gist: Congress legalizes outsourcing intelligence work to private firms, and Greg, trapped and complicit, learns Maya has died abroad before being pressured back to his desk inside Google's secret unit.

children.title: Afterword to the story
children.gist: Doctorow says Radar commissioned a story on how Google might turn evil, and he wanted to show good people enabling harm through a compelling business and technical logic rather than cartoonish villainy.
